hints: Focus on the two $\text{-OH}$ groups in $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and what type of intermolecular force they always allow.
Remember ice is a giant lattice of water molecules held by hydrogen bonds, so think how a new hydrogen-bonding molecule would disrupt it.
Connect hydrogen bonding to solubility by asking if ethylene glycol can bond to water and to itself in the same way.
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of ice**

Ice is water in a rigid, extensive 3D network of hydrogen bonds. To melt it below $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, something must disrupt that network.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{H bonded to O, N or F + lone pair on O, N or F} \rightarrow \text{hydrogen bond}$$

**Check what ethylene glycol can do**

$\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ has two hydroxyl $\text{-OH}$ groups. Each $\text{O-H}$ can donate a hydrogen bond, and each O can accept hydrogen bonds.

That means it can hydrogen bond to water, to ice, and to other ethylene glycol molecules. So statement 1 and statement 2 are both true.

**Explain dissolving and de-icing**

Like dissolves like. A small molecule with two $\text{-OH}$ groups mixes very well with water by forming new hydrogen bonds to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Once a little water forms, ethylene glycol dissolves in it, prevents water reforming the perfect ice lattice, and lowers the freezing point. So statement 3 is also true, and 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: Correct. All three statements are true. Ethylene glycol disrupts the hydrogen-bonded ice lattice (1), hydrogen bonds to itself via its -OH groups (2), and dissolves in water by hydrogen bonding to water (3).
options.B: Incorrect. This combination includes only 1 and 2. It wrongly leaves out statement 3. Students choose this if they forget that two -OH groups make ethylene glycol fully miscible with water.
options.C: Incorrect. This combination includes only 2 and 3. It wrongly leaves out statement 1. The whole de-icer action depends on disrupting the hydrogen bond network in ice, so 1 must be included.
options.D: Incorrect. This is statement 1 only. It misses that hydrogen bonding also occurs between ethylene glycol molecules themselves and between ethylene glycol and liquid water.
